guide.title: Parione, Rome: Piazza Navona, Campo de' Fiori and the Cancelleria
guide.intro: Parione is the sixth of Rome's rioni, a wedge of the centro storico with Piazza Navona at one end and Campo de' Fiori at the other. Between the two squares the rione is working streets — Via del Pellegrino, Via dei Cappellari, Via di Grotta Pinta, whose bend still follows the seating of Pompey's theatre. It also holds the Palazzo della Cancelleria, which the Lateran Treaty names among the Holy See's properties standing on Italian soil. Almost every edge of Parione is shared with a neighbouring rione, so several things visitors place here are not here: Santa Maria della Pace and Santa Maria dell'Anima are contested between rioni, and this guide does not carry them.

sections.heading: The edges
sections.body: Parione's southern edge is Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, a cut driven through the older fabric, and it is shared with three other rioni — Ponte, Sant'Eustachio and Pigna. The Museo Barracco at corso Vittorio Emanuele 166/A, San Pantaleo and Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne stand in Parione. The Oratorio dei Filippini is inside Parione, and the Piazza dell'Orologio it addresses from is mostly in rione Ponte; the Oratory, the Biblioteca Vallicelliana and the Archivio Storico Capitolino share the one building. Campo de' Fiori sits on the line between Parione and Regola, and it.wikipedia declares that boundary itself; part of the Chiesa Nuova falls in Ponte. Santa Maria della Pace, its cloister and Santa Maria dell'Anima are contested between rioni. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the Fontana della Terrina stood at the centre of Campo de' Fiori until it was dismantled for the Giordano Bruno monument, and was rebuilt in 1924 before the Chiesa Nuova; the Sovrintendenza Capitolina and it.wikipedia give different accounts of where it now stands. No source states a legal protection status for any building in Parione.

sections.heading: The Cancelleria, the Lateran Treaty and UNESCO
sections.body: The Palazzo della Cancelleria has an unusual legal position, and it is easy to get wrong. Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929 names it among buildings which, in the treaty's own words, although forming part of the territory of the Italian State, enjoy the immunities that international law recognises for the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. That is the immunity of a diplomatic headquarters, granted on Italian soil. The palazzo is not part of Vatican City, it is not Vatican territory, it is not a border, and a visitor standing outside it is in Italy and subject to Italian law. It remains the property of the Holy See and houses the Apostolic Penitentiary, the Apostolic Signatura and the Roman Rota. The basilica of San Lorenzo in Damaso is incorporated into the palace, its main door set in the right-hand part of the façade — and nothing this guide could reach says anything about the basilica's own legal position, so it says nothing. On the wider record: the Historic Centre of Rome, the Properties of the Holy See in that City Enjoying Extraterritorial Rights and San Paolo Fuori le Mura was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980, as site 91, with a significant boundary modification in 1990 and minor modifications in 2015 and 2023, under criteria (i)(ii)(iii)(iv)(vi), over a property of 1,469.7 hectares. UNESCO's own description of the site names Piazza Navona by name among the Renaissance and Baroque urban developments of the historic centre. It does not name the Cancelleria, or any other individual Parione building.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: This guide publishes no walking times and no distance it has not taken from a source, so steer by street numbers rather than by an impression of how far apart things are. Its southern edge is Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, which carries the addresses of two of the rione's institutions. The addresses worth having, each taken from the institution's own website: the Museo di Roma in Palazzo Braschi gives two entrances, Piazza San Pantaleo 10 and Piazza Navona 2; the Museo Barracco gives corso Vittorio Emanuele 166/A; the Archivio Storico Capitolino gives Piazza dell'Orologio 4. All three are 00186 Roma. To orient yourself on the eastern side, the church of Nostra Signora del Sacro Cuore has its front on corso del Rinascimento and its rear façade on Piazza Navona, so the two run parallel with the church between them. No source names a metro station inside Parione, so none is given.

faq.question: Is Piazza Navona in Parione?
faq.answer: Yes, and wholly so — the square lies entirely inside the rione. UNESCO's description of the Historic Centre of Rome names Piazza Navona among the site's Renaissance and Baroque urban developments.

faq.question: Is Campo de' Fiori in Parione?
faq.answer: Partly. it.wikipedia places the square between via dei Giubbonari and piazza della Cancelleria, on the boundary of the rioni Parione and Regola, and carries both rione categories on the same article. Most of it falls in Parione, but the market and the monument to Giordano Bruno in it are not wholly Parione's.

faq.question: Can I go into the Stadium of Domitian under Piazza Navona?
faq.answer: Not at present. The whole of what the archaeological area's own website carries is a notice, in four languages, that the area is currently closed to the public, directing enquiries to the Sovrintendenza Capitolina ai Beni Culturali. It gives no hours, no address and no ticket, so none are given.

faq.question: Is the Palazzo della Cancelleria part of the Vatican?
faq.answer: No. Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty says the opposite in its own words: the buildings it names form part of the territory of the Italian State, and what they are granted is the immunity international law gives to the seats of foreign diplomatic agents. The palazzo is not Vatican City, not Vatican territory and not a border, and anyone visiting it is in Italy and subject to Italian law.

faq.question: Is Santa Maria della Pace in Parione?
faq.answer: No. Three independent methods put Santa Maria della Pace in rione Ponte, including it.wikipedia's own prose, which says it stands in the square of the same name in rione Ponte. Santa Maria dell'Anima is in Ponte too, though the evidence there is genuinely split. Neither is carried in this guide, and rione Ponte has not been written yet.

faq.question: What does the Museo di Roma cost, and where do you go in?
faq.answer: The museum occupies Palazzo Braschi and has two entrances, at Piazza San Pantaleo 10 and Piazza Navona 2. Entry is free for MIC-card holders, with separate ticketing for the exhibition space; the museum gives 060608, 9.00-19.00, for information and booking. Its collections cover the social history and artistic activity of Rome from the Middle Ages to the early 20th century.

photos.title: Piazza Navona
photos.description: The west side of Piazza Navona, with the facade of Sant'Agnese in Agone, the Palazzo Pamphilj alongside it, and the Obelisco Agonale rising over the Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi at right.
photos.author: Wolfgang Moroder

places.name: Piazza Navona
places.summary: Piazza Navona takes the shape of the ancient stadium beneath it, and was given its monumental form for Innocent X (Giovanni Battista Pamphilj). UNESCO names Piazza Navona among the Renaissance and Baroque urban developments of the Historic Centre of Rome (World Heritage site 91).
places.history: Three fountains stand along the length of the square — the Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi at the centre, the Fontana del Moro, and the Fontana del Nettuno — together with the church of Sant'Agnese in Agone and the Palazzo Pamphilj. The square is wholly inside rione Parione, which is not true of most of Parione's edges.

places.name: Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi
places.summary: The fountain at the centre of Piazza Navona. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives its author as Gian Lorenzo Bernini and its date as 1648-1651, and its materials as travertine, marble, granite and bronze. It was originally fed by the acqua Vergine.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza's account: Innocent X commissioned the fountain, which replaced a trough installed with the square's two side fountains in the 1570s. In 1647 the pope gave Borromini the new conduit that brought 180 once of Acqua Vergine to the piazza, and had the obelisk moved in. Bernini won the commission having presented a silver model.

places.name: Obelisco Agonale
places.summary: The obelisk crowning the fountain is described by the Sovrintendenza Capitolina as a Roman copy of Domitianic date; before Innocent X moved it to the square it lay in pieces in the area of the Circus of Maxentius on the Via Appia Antica.

places.name: Fontana del Moro
places.summary: The Fontana del Moro stands in Piazza Navona. it.wikipedia gives the basin to Giacomo della Porta and the figure of the Moor to a design by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, executed by Giovanni Antonio Mari. This guide attributes those to it.wikipedia rather than asserting them, and publishes nothing about who paid for the work.

places.name: Fontana del Nettuno
places.summary: The basin of this fountain, in Piazza Navona, is attributed to Giacomo della Porta. The Neptune group standing above it is a much later addition, so this guide gives the basin an attribution and the group none.

places.name: Sant'Agnese in Agone
places.summary: The church on the west side of Piazza Navona, dedicated to St Agnes on the traditional site of her martyrdom. it.wikipedia attributes the building to Carlo Rainaldi and Francesco Borromini; this guide attributes rather than states it.
places.history: The parish keeps a live website of its own, which is what establishes the church's identity, its location and the functions held in it, and which publishes its opening times. The parish also sets out a restoration programme in the crypt — that is the parish's own statement about its own building.

places.name: Palazzo Pamphilj
places.summary: The long palace on Piazza Navona, built for the Pamphilj family in the mid-17th century. it.wikipedia's prose gives the architect as Girolamo Rainaldi.
places.history: The palace is used by the Pamphilj family as a private residence and as the embassy of Brazil to the Italian State. It is a working diplomatic building, not a visitor attraction, and this guide makes no claim about access to it.

places.name: Stadio di Domiziano
places.summary: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records the Stadium in Rione VI Parione. Its operator's website states that the archaeological area is currently closed to the public.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza's description of the building: the Circus Agonalis, 265 by 106 metres, circus-shaped but differing from a circus in its smaller size and in having neither spina nor obelisk; an exterior of two tiers of arcades on piers, Ionic below and Corinthian above, with an entrance on each side; construction in travertine block and brick facing, the interior walls in soberly decorated stucco. Its walls re-emerged in 1936 during demolition and rebuilding work on the emiciclo, and after full excavation the remains were incorporated into the Palazzo dell'INA. Piazza Navona above it keeps the stadium's outline.

places.name: Chiesa di Nostra Signora del Sacro Cuore
places.summary: A church that faces two ways: its front is on corso del Rinascimento and its rear façade is on Piazza Navona. The two streets run parallel with the church between them, which is how the square sits behind corso del Rinascimento.

places.name: Palazzo De Torres-Lancellotti
places.summary: The palace's main front is on Piazza Navona; its other sides stand on via della Cuccagna, via della Posta Vecchia, vicolo della Cuccagna and piazza de' Massimi.
places.history: it.wikipedia derives the name of via della Cuccagna from the albero della cuccagna, the greased pole; the derivation is attributed here rather than asserted.

places.name: San Nicola dei Lorenesi
places.summary: The church stands in Largo Febo. it.wikipedia records that after the annexation of Lorraine to France in 1766 it was integrated into the Pieux Établissements de la France à Rome et Lorette, and that it is one of the five French Catholic churches in Rome, named alongside San Luigi dei Francesi, Trinità dei Monti, Sant'Ivo dei Bretoni and Santi Claudio e Andrea dei Borgognoni.
places.history: No source states the architect. The only aggregator field offering one resolves to a person who could not have built it, which is a good reason to resolve every such field to a name before trusting it.

places.name: Pasquino
places.summary: Pasquino became a characteristic figure of the city between the 16th and 19th centuries. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the statue is traditionally referred to the decoration of the Stadium of Domitian, that it was found in Piazza Navona at the corner with Via della Cuccagna, and that it represents the group of Patroclus and Menelaus - while noting that other statues certainly belonging to the Stadium's decoration were found in other excavations around it.
places.history: The statue stands in the small square that takes its name, Piazza di Pasquino.

places.name: Palazzo Braschi
places.summary: it.wikipedia locates Palazzo Braschi in R. VI Parione, between piazza San Pantaleo, via San Pantaleo, via della Cuccagna, via di Pasquino and piazza Navona — a rione statement in the source's own words, which is what settles the location here.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina calls the building eighteenth-century. This guide gives no single construction year, because the only source offering one gives a year that a second source's description cannot accommodate. it.wikipedia records that the palace has housed the Museo di Roma since 1952.

places.name: Museo di Roma
places.summary: The Museo di Roma occupies Palazzo Braschi, with entrances at Piazza San Pantaleo 10 and Piazza Navona 2. Its collections cover the social history and artistic activity of Rome from the Middle Ages to the early 20th century. Entry is free for MIC-card holders, with separate ticketing for the exhibition space; information and booking on 060608, 9.00-19.00.

places.name: Chiesa della Natività di Gesù
places.summary: The church faces piazza Pasquino, in rione Parione, and is the national church of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the church was built at the end of the 17th century, and that it took its present form in a restoration of 1862 by Andrea Busiri Vici. The 1862 date is the restoration, not the foundation.

places.name: Palazzo della Cancelleria
places.summary: The Palazzo della Cancelleria stands in Parione, on Italian soil. Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty of 1929 names it among the buildings which, in the treaty's own words, although forming part of the territory of the Italian State, enjoy the immunities that international law recognises for the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign states. It is not part of Vatican City and it is not a border; visitors there are in Italy. It remains the property of the Holy See and houses the Apostolic Penitentiary, the Apostolic Signatura and the Roman Rota.
places.history: This guide gives the palazzo no construction date and no architect. The sources we hold disagree three ways with one another, and one of them has plainly read a later event as a building date, so nothing about the building's origin can be published with a straight face. The UNESCO record for the Historic Centre of Rome does not name this building individually, and no claim is made here that it does.

places.name: San Lorenzo in Damaso
places.summary: The basilica stands in rione Parione, incorporated into the Palazzo della Cancelleria, with its main entrance set into the right-hand part of the palace façade.
places.history: No source states anything about the basilica's own legal position, so this guide states nothing about it. The immunities Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty describes are granted to the named palazzi, and nothing we hold extends them to the church inside one.

places.name: Campo de' Fiori
places.summary: Campo de' Fiori lies between via dei Giubbonari and piazza della Cancelleria, on the boundary of the rioni Parione and Regola. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes the square as the seat of a city market.
places.history: Most of the square falls in Parione, and it.wikipedia declares the boundary between Parione and Regola itself. Neither the market nor the monument standing in the square is wholly Parione's.

places.name: Monumento a Giordano Bruno
places.summary: The bronze and Baveno granite figure standing in Campo de' Fiori, on the boundary of Parione and Regola. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives its author as Ettore Ferrari (1845-1929) and records that it was raised on 9 June 1889, on the site of the burning of Giordano Bruno on 17 February 1600.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza's account of how it got there: two international university committees, in 1876 and 1884, raised the money; the Comune di Roma raised no objection to the site in 1877 and gave a modest contribution; by 1887, with a clerical majority on the Campidoglio, the siting had become a political battle for liberal and anticlerical opinion. Ferrari's first version of 1879, showing Bruno defiant before the Inquisition, was rejected; the version built was the 1887 proposal, the philosopher drawn into himself with his hands crossed on his book.

places.name: Fontana di Campo de' Fiori
places.summary: The fountain now in the square is a 19th-century copy of the basin Giacomo della Porta designed for it. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the copy was placed in 1898, during the repaving of the square, on ground that had been occupied by buildings until 1858, on the side toward via dei Cappellari, via del Pellegrino and piazza della Cancelleria. It is fed by the acqua Paola and reproduces Della Porta's basin in size and proportion, without the 17th-century lid.
places.history: The date is the Sovrintendenza's. it.wikipedia dates the copy to 1924 instead; where Roma Capitale's own page and an aggregator disagree, this guide follows Roma Capitale and says whose date it is using.

places.name: Palazzo Orsini Pio Righetti
places.summary: The palace on the south side of Campo de' Fiori, also known as Palazzo Pio. It stands over the substructures of the Theatre of Pompey.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on Campo de' Fiori carries the ownership chain, attributed to it rather than asserted: the Orsini, then the Pio di Savoia, who rebuilt the palace entirely, then the Righetti. No source gives a single construction year.

places.name: Teatro di Pompeo
places.summary: it.wikipedia describes the Theatre of Pompey as the theatrum marmoreum, and states that the site today belongs to the rione Parione. The curve of its cavea survives in the line of the houses along Via di Grotta Pinta.
places.history: There is nothing to go inside. What there is to see is the street plan: walk Via di Grotta Pinta and the bend of the houses is the shape of the seating. The buildings above and around it — the Palazzo Orsini Pio Righetti, the deconsecrated church of Santa Maria in Grottapinta — sit on the theatre's substructures.

places.name: Santa Maria in Grottapinta
places.summary: A deconsecrated church in rione Parione, facing the piazza of the same name. it.wikipedia records that it was built on the foundations of the inner corridor of the Theatre of Pompey.
places.history: No foundation date is given: the source says outright that the date is not known.

places.name: Museo Barracco
places.summary: The Museo di scultura antica Giovanni Barracco gives its address as corso Vittorio Emanuele 166/A, 00186 Roma, telephone 060608. Its collection of ancient sculpture, classical and Ancient Near Eastern, was donated to the Comune by Giovanni Barracco in 1904. Entry is free for MIC-card holders; information and booking on 060608, 9.00-19.00.
places.history: The building stands in rione Parione even though it addresses onto corso Vittorio Emanuele II, which is shared between four rioni and belongs to none of them in this corpus.

places.name: Farnesina ai Baullari (Palazzetto Le Roy)
places.summary: The palazzetto that houses the Museo Barracco. That is the whole of what this guide publishes about it: no date, no architect, no independent standing.
places.history: A warning for readers and for anyone editing this corpus later: the Farnesina ai Baullari is not the Villa Farnesina. They are two different buildings, in two different rioni, with confusingly similar names, and this entry refers only to the small palazzo on corso Vittorio Emanuele that the Museo Barracco occupies.

places.name: Santa Barbara dei Librai
places.summary: The church stands precisely in Largo dei Librari. it.wikipedia records that it is also called Santa Barbara alla Regola, from the rione it anciently belonged to — a documented change of rione, and a useful reminder that these boundaries have moved.

places.name: Arco degli Acetari
places.summary: it.wikipedia places the Arco degli Acetari in Rione Parione, along Via del Pellegrino, and describes it as leading to an inner courtyard ringed by buildings of medieval origin.
places.history: That is deliberately all. The source article is thin and largely built on a single non-institutional citation, so this guide publishes the location and the courtyard and treats everything else about it as unsourced.

places.name: Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne
places.address: Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The palace stands on corso Vittorio Emanuele II, in Parione.
places.history: Wikidata gives the date as 1532 and the architect as Baldassare Peruzzi; both are attributed here rather than asserted, because that field is the only place either appears. it.wikipedia records that the site faced the Via Sacra, or Via Papale, from the 12th century.

places.name: San Pantaleo
places.summary: San Pantaleo stands in rione Parione, facing its own piazza along corso Vittorio Emanuele II. it.wikipedia records that the church was rebuilt between 1681 and 1689 to a design by Giovanni Antonio De Rossi, and that its neoclassical façade, of the early 19th century, is the work of Giuseppe Valadier.

places.name: Chiesa Nuova (Santa Maria in Vallicella)
places.address: Piazza della Chiesa Nuova, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The Chiesa Nuova stands on the piazza of the same name in rione Parione, on the boundary line with rione Ponte — it.wikipedia records that part of the building falls in Ponte.
places.history: Rione Ponte has not been written for this corpus yet. When it is, the part of this building that stands in it will need looking at again; the church is published once, here, so that it cannot end up in two places at the same time.

places.name: Oratorio dei Filippini
places.summary: it.wikipedia records that the Oratorio dei Filippini was built by Francesco Borromini between 1637 and 1667, commissioned by the Congregation of the Oratory of St Philip Neri. Borromini's clock tower — the Torre dell'Orologio — stands on the same complex.
places.history: The building addresses from Piazza dell'Orologio and stands in Parione. The Biblioteca Vallicelliana, on its second floor, and the Archivio Storico Capitolino are inside it.

places.name: Biblioteca Vallicelliana
places.address: Piazza della Chiesa Nuova, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: it.wikipedia places the Biblioteca Vallicelliana in piazza della Chiesa Nuova, in rione Parione, beside the church of Santa Maria in Vallicella and on the second floor of the Oratorio dei Filippini — Borromini's 17th-century building.
places.history: No source states the library's opening hours, its access rules or its founding date, so none of those are given here. What this guide publishes is where the library is and what building it is in.

places.name: Archivio Storico Capitolino
places.summary: The Archivio Storico Capitolino occupies the Oratorio dei Filippini and gives its address as Piazza dell'Orologio, 4 - 00186 Roma, telephone 06 67 10 81 00. Its own site states that access to the public is free. It holds the documentation produced by the comune di Roma.
places.history: One caveat is the archive's own, and it saves a wasted journey: for a building, it holds only the files of projects actually built in Rome. The archive is a section of the Sovrintendenza Capitolina ai Beni Culturali, which lists it among its own. No source states its current opening hours, so none are given here.

places.name: Monumento a Pietro Metastasio
places.address: Piazza della Chiesa Nuova, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The monument to Pietro Metastasio stands in piazza della Chiesa Nuova. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that it was promoted by a committee of artists formed in 1873 under Francesco Podesti, director of the Accademia di San Luca, for the centenary of the poet's death; that the competition was held in 1882 and won by the sculptor Emilio Gallori; that it was inaugurated in piazza San Silvestro on 21 April 1886; and that it was moved to piazza della Chiesa Nuova in 1910, during the works along the line of corso Vittorio Emanuele II. The poet's birthplace was at via dei Cappellari 30, and the monument faces the Oratory of the Filippini, where sacred melodramas were performed.
places.history: No birth year is given for the sculptor: the Sovrintendenza's own page contradicts itself between its header and its body, so this guide publishes neither.

places.name: San Tommaso in Parione
places.summary: The national church of the Eritrean Catholic community in Rome, of the Alexandrian rite, in rione Parione.

entries.name: Piazza Navona
entries.note: The square keeps the outline of the ancient stadium beneath it, and lies wholly inside the rione, which is not true of most of Parione's edges.

entries.name: Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi
entries.note: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives it to Gian Lorenzo Bernini and dates it 1648-1651, in travertine, marble, granite and bronze, on the site of a trough from the 1570s.

entries.name: Sant'Agnese in Agone
entries.note: The church on Piazza Navona, on the traditional site of St Agnes's martyrdom; the parish publishes its own opening times and a restoration programme in the crypt.

entries.name: Stadio di Domiziano
entries.note: The archaeological area is closed to the public, so plan to read the stadium from the piazza above rather than from inside; the walls re-emerged in 1936 and were built into the Palazzo dell'INA.

entries.name: Pasquino
entries.note: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina reads the battered group as Patroclus and Menelaus, found at the corner of Piazza Navona and Via della Cuccagna, and refers it to the Stadium's decoration.

entries.name: Museo di Roma
entries.note: Collections covering the social history and artistic activity of Rome from the Middle Ages to the early 20th century, with entrances at Piazza San Pantaleo 10 and Piazza Navona 2.

entries.name: Museo Barracco
entries.note: Classical and Ancient Near Eastern sculpture, given to the Comune by Giovanni Barracco in 1904, at corso Vittorio Emanuele 166/A.

entries.name: Palazzo della Cancelleria
entries.note: Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty of 1929 grants it the immunities international law recognises for the seats of foreign diplomatic agents, on Italian soil; it houses the Apostolic Penitentiary, the Apostolic Signatura and the Roman Rota.

entries.name: Campo de' Fiori
entries.note: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes it as the seat of a city market; it runs between via dei Giubbonari and piazza della Cancelleria, on the Parione-Regola boundary.

entries.name: Monumento a Giordano Bruno
entries.note: Ettore Ferrari's bronze and Baveno granite figure, raised on 9 June 1889 on the site of the burning of 17 February 1600, with the philosopher drawn into himself and his hands crossed on his book.

entries.name: Teatro di Pompeo
entries.note: There is nothing to go inside; walk Via di Grotta Pinta and the bend of the houses is the line of the seating.

entries.name: Arco degli Acetari
entries.note: An opening off Via del Pellegrino leading to an inner courtyard ringed by buildings of medieval origin.

entries.name: Oratorio dei Filippini
entries.note: it.wikipedia gives it to Francesco Borromini, 1637-1667, for the Congregation of the Oratory; his Torre dell'Orologio stands on the same complex, and the Biblioteca Vallicelliana and the Archivio Storico Capitolino are inside it.

links.note: Parione's neighbour along corso Vittorio Emanuele II, a cut that four rioni divide between them and that this corpus gives to none of them.
Another rione of Municipio I in this series. It holds the Palazzo di Propaganda Fide, another Lateran Treaty property standing on Italian soil.
Another rione of Municipio I in this series, covering the Trevi Fountain and the Quirinal.
